questions.q: Where are the people of Israel preparing to go?
questions.a: Israel is about to cross over the Jordan.

questions.q: What will happen when Israel crosses Jordan?
questions.a: Yahweh will go ahead of them and will destroy the nations like a devouring fire.

questions.q: What did Moses tell the people not to think after Yahweh enables them to drive their enemies out of the land?
questions.a: He told them not to think that it was because of Israel’s righteousness that Yahweh gave them the land.

questions.q: What is the reason God is driving the nations out?
questions.a: He is driving them out because of their wickedness, and to keep his promise to Israel’s ancestors, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

questions.q: Why was Yahweh angry with the people of Israel?
questions.a: He was angry with them because they were rebellious against him.

questions.q: What did Moses eat and drink on the mountain?
questions.a: He did not eat or drink anything for 40 days and 40 nights on the mountain.

questions.q: Why did Yahweh tell Moses to quickly go down from the mountain?
questions.a: Yahweh told him the people had corrupted themselves by doing what Yahweh had commanded them not to do and had made for themselves an idol to worship.

questions.q: Why did Yahweh say he would destroy the Israelites?
questions.a: Yahweh said he had seen that they were a stubborn people.

questions.q: What did Moses find that Israel had made while he was on the mountain?
questions.a: They had sinned against Yahweh by molding a calf as an idol just as he had commanded them not to do.

questions.q: What did Moses do after he saw that the people had done evil in the sight of Yahweh?
questions.a: He threw down the tablets and broke them before their eyes, he prostrated himself before Yahweh for 40 days and nights, and did not eat or drink because of their sin.

questions.q: Why did Moses pray for the people and Aaron?
questions.a: He prayed because Yahweh was angry enough with the people and with Aaron to destroy them.

questions.q: What did Moses do to the calf that the people had made?
questions.a: Moses burned it, crushed it, and ground it into dust and threw the dust into the stream that came down from the mountain.

questions.q: How did the people provoke Yahweh to anger?
questions.a: They rebelled against the commandment of Yahweh by not trusting him or obeying what he told them.

questions.q: What was Moses praying as he prostrated himself before Yahweh for 40 days and nights?
questions.a: He prayed that Yahweh would not destroy his people whom he had rescued and brought out of Egypt.

questions.q: What was Moses thinking the people of Egypt would say if Yahweh destroyed his people?
questions.a: He is afraid the people of Egypt would say that Yahweh was not able to bring Israel into the land he had promised them but that he took them into the wilderness to kill them because he hated them.

commentary.text: The Israelites not to think their success came by their own worthiness.
Moses reminds the Israelites of their rebellions.

Verses 1–6 Moses represents the strength of the enemies they were now to encounter. This was to drive them to God, and engage their hope in him. He assures them of victory, by the presence of God with them. He cautions them not to have the least thought of their own righteousness, as if that procured this favour at God's hand. In Christ we have both righteousness and strength; in Him we must glory, not in ourselves, nor in any sufficiency of our own. It is for the wickedness of these nations that God drives them out. All whom God rejects, are rejected for their own wickedness; but none whom he accepts are accepted for their own righteousness. Thus boasting is for ever done away: see Eph 2:9, 11, 12.

That the Israelites might have no pretence to think that God brought them to Canaan for their righteousness, Moses shows what a miracle of mercy it was, that they had not been destroyed in the wilderness. It is good for us often to remember against ourselves, with sorrow and shame, our former sins; that we may see how much we are indebted to free grace, and may humbly own that we never merited any thing but wrath and the curse at God's hand. For so strong is our propensity to pride, that it will creep in under one pretence or another. We are ready to fancy that our righteousness has got for us the special favour of the Lord, though in reality our wickedness is more plain than our weakness. But when the secret history of every man's life shall be brought forth at the day of judgment, all the world will be proved guilty before God. At present, One pleads for us before the mercy-seat, who not only fasted, but died upon the cross for our sins; through whom we may approach, though self-condemned sinners, and beseech for undeserved mercy and for eternal life, as the gift of God in Him. Let us refer all the victory, all the glory, and all the praise, to Him who alone bringeth salvation.
